title: Google Cloud races to catch up in the AI deployment wars with Accenture deal
content:
Google Cloud and Accenture are working together on a joint unit dedicated to sending engineers into enterprises to help them better adopt Google’s AI tools and services.
The new unit, dubbed Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group, is Google’s latest foray into the increasingly competitive world of “forward-deployed engineers,” or FDEs. Rivals in the AI race, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Amazon, have all recently launched separate business units in a bet that implementing AI models can become its own trillion-dollar business.
It’s the kind of bet AI companies and hyperscalers increasingly need to make. Hyperscalers are committing hundreds of billions of dollars a year to GPUs, data centers, and power capacity even as the revenue directly attributable to AI remains a fraction of that investment.
Google Cloud generated $24.8 billion in the second quarter, a big chunk of which was driven by enterprise AI. But the commitments behind that growth are enormous. Google Cloud’s parent company Alphabet reportedly accumulated $811 billion in purchase commitments and contractual obligations as of June 30.
This return on investment is not yet materializing in the way companies and investors need it to, so everything hinges on whether or not AI companies can create enough demand for their services. But that demand is not guaranteed, as enterprises themselves are struggling to see a true return on investment on their AI spending.
It’s conventionally held that enterprises have simply lacked the expertise to intelligently integrate AI tools and services into their workflows in a way that not only saves them money, but helps them make more of it in the long run. That’s where the FDEs come in as a steady, guiding hand that, ideally, possesses the perfect mental cocktail of business acumen and agentic AI prowess needed to change everything.
As part of its deal with Accenture, Google will train up to 1,000 of the consultancy firm’s FDEs to work with enterprises and build custom AI applications on the Gemini Enterprise platform.
According to August data from Ramp, Google accounts for roughly 6% of enterprise AI spending among U.S. businesses, compared to Anthropic’s 43.5% and OpenAI’s 39.7%. Google’s new unit with Accenture, which The Wall Street Journal first reported, is the latest of its aggressive expansions of its FDE model this year as it attempts to resolve enterprise deployment bottlenecks and catch up to rivals.
Earlier this year, Google Cloud launched a $750 million partner ecosystem commitment that embedded Google’s own FDEs across multiple consultancies, including Capgemini, Cognizant and Deloitte. The tech giant also struck a multi-year partnership with CVC Capital Partners to deploy FDEs directly into the investment firm’s portfolio companies.
Google isn’t the only giant at risk of being outpaced by newer firms. Companies that are dedicated specifically to embedding engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI workflows — like Ode with Anthropic, or OpenAI’s The Deployment Co. — threaten big consultancy firms like Accenture as well. For the professional services giant, the Google tie-up adds to its own wave of FDE programs this year, which include a similar Microsoft FDE practice in March, an FDE initiative with ServiceNow in May, and a joint program with SAP in June.

report.summary: Google Cloud partners with Accenture to deploy 1,000 forward-deployed engineers, aiming to close the enterprise AI adoption gap against rivals.
report.background: Cloud providers and AI labs are spending hundreds of billions on GPUs and data centers, but AI revenue remains a small fraction of that investment. Enterprises, meanwhile, struggle to see meaningful ROI from AI because they lack the internal expertise to integrate models into real workflows. That gap has sparked a new competitive arena: 'forward-deployed engineers' (FDEs) who embed directly with clients to build custom AI applications. Google Cloud, despite strong Q2 revenue, captures only about 6% of U.S. enterprise AI spending, far behind Anthropic and OpenAI. The Accenture tie-up is Google's latest effort to accelerate adoption and catch up in what is becoming a trillion-dollar deployment market.
key_points: Google and Accenture have created the Accenture Gemini Enterprise Business Group, a joint unit focused on enterprise AI deployment. Google will train up to 1,000 Accenture engineers to build custom applications using the Gemini Enterprise platform, giving enterprises a guided path to integrating Google's AI tools.

The deal is driven by a massive ROI gap. Hyperscalers carry enormous capital commitments—Alphabet reported $811 billion in purchase obligations as of June 30—while AI-related revenue is still relatively small. To justify these bets, AI vendors must help enterprises find real, monetizable use cases rather than just selling model access.

Google is far behind in enterprise AI spending: Ramp data shows Google has only 6% of U.S. enterprise AI spend, compared with Anthropic's 43.5% and OpenAI's 39.7%. The Accenture partnership is part of an aggressive FDE expansion to remove deployment bottlenecks and close that competitive gap.

This is not Google's first FDE push this year. Earlier, Google Cloud committed $750 million to embed its own engineers across consultancies like Capgemini, Cognizant, and Deloitte, and it partnered with CVC Capital Partners to deploy FDEs into portfolio companies. The Accenture unit is a larger, more focused escalation of that strategy.

Professional services firms face threats from specialized AI deployment outfits like Anthropic-backed Ode and OpenAI's The Deployment Co. Accenture itself has launched FDE practices with Microsoft, ServiceNow, and SAP, making partnerships with multiple AI vendors a defensive and offensive move in a fast-evolving market.
report.impact: This signals that the AI industry's competitive frontier is shifting from model performance to real-world deployment. For AI companies, success now depends on demonstrating ROI at the enterprise level, not just releasing better benchmarks. Developers can expect more demand for hybrid skills: business analysis plus agentic AI engineering. For regular users, this means more customized AI applications and smoother integration into daily workflows, but also risks of vendor lock-in and opaque costs as consultancies push specific platforms. Smaller AI-native firms may face pressure as giants bundle deployment services with their models, potentially consolidating the market around those who can offer both technology and hands-on implementation.
report.tools: For those tracking this space, watch Google's Gemini Enterprise platform and Accenture's Google Cloud practice. Also monitor Anthropic's Ode and OpenAI's The Deployment Co. for comparison. Developers experimenting with agentic workflows can explore open-source frameworks like LangChain and LangGraph, or Google's own Agent Development Kit, to build similar custom enterprise AI applications.
